column4: The definition of righteousness gathers giving beloved wealth to kin, orphans, and the needy, giving it “في الرقاب,” and steadfastness; it is the closest Quranic gathering of the section’s freed neck, feeding, and self-restraint.
The battle command moves from striking “الرقاب” to tightening the bond and then either gracious release or ransom, staging in one ayah the neck, the tightened tie, and its possible opening.
The expiation of a binding oath is feeding or clothing ten poor people or “تحرير رقبة”; release from a verbal bond is enacted by feeding or releasing a human neck.
Enslaved people seeking a manumission contract are to receive both the contract and some of the wealth God gave their owners, making wealth the means by which ownership’s bond is opened.
For an accidental killing, “تحرير رقبة مؤمنة” restores a believing human life through the release of another believing person represented by the neck.
The assigned uses of alms include “وفي الرقاب,” so wealth is expressly redirected from possession toward freeing possessed persons.
The one retracting ẓihār must perform “تحرير رقبة” before the couple touch, placing release of a neck before release from the speaker’s own binding utterance.
The Messenger removes people’s burdens and “الأغلال التي كانت عليهم”; guidance here is an act of taking off bonds, the saving direction of the section’s opening motion.

The Quran’s other occurrence of the section’s ف ك ك root says the disbelievers were not “منفكين” until the clear proof came; separation or release is placed beside the very covering of truth discussed in the section.
“كل نفس بما كسبت رهينة” makes every soul collateral for what it earns, directly activating the section’s locked pledge and asking what can effect its release.
The exception “إلا أصحاب اليمين” follows the pledged soul of 74:38 and names the same saved company that the surah places beyond the steep ascent and the freed neck.
A journey without a scribe may require “فرهان مقبوضة,” collateral physically taken into possession; this is the Quranic legal scene behind the source section’s pledge locked until فك opens it.
After promising believing families reunion, the ayah says every person is “بما كسب رهين”; kinship cannot erase each person’s own pledged accountability.
The other Quranic “مؤصدة” says the fire is closed over the wealth-counter and slanderer, exactly repeating the section’s punitive lid.
“في عمد ممددة” supplies the extended columns of 104:8’s closure, giving the closed fire a structural image rather than merely naming confinement.
The dog stretches its forelegs “بالوصيد,” using the section’s و ص د family for the cave’s threshold or entrance, the spatial edge from which the same root’s closing sense develops.
Moses asks God “واحلل عقدة من لساني”; the section’s dictionary definition of حل as untying a knot becomes an explicit Quranic act that releases speech.
The nearer life is vegetation after rain whose growth pleases “الكفار”; here the section’s secondary كافر, the farmer who covers seed, is present in a scene of growth that soon dries and breaks.
The righteous feed food they love to a poor person, an orphan, and “أسيرا”; care reaches the captive rather than tightening captivity.
Those who cover their Lord’s truth have “الأغلال في أعناقهم” and are companions of the fire, joining disbelief, earth, neck-fetters, and final enclosure in one ayah.
The disputants are dragged with fetters “في أعناقهم” and chains, turning the neck that could have been freed into the point by which the whole person is hauled.
Immediately after the way is shown in 76:3, the rejecters receive chains, fetters, and a blaze; their response to guidance determines whether bondage or grateful action follows.
Fetters are placed “في أعناقهم” up to their chins, making the neck-bond force the entire body into a fixed posture.
“خذوه فغلوه” orders that the unbelieving, ungenerous person be seized and fettered, the punitive reversal of taking hold of a bound person in order to free them.
This ayah casts the seized person of 69:30 into Hellfire, joining his fetter to the enclosing fire whose cause the following ayat disclose.
The command to insert him into a seventy-cubit chain completes the physical binding begun in 69:30.
His chain and fire are explained by the fact that he did not believe in God, matching the section’s movement from covering truth to being covered.
He also did not urge feeding the needy; the failure to loosen hunger for another returns as the chain imposed on himself in 69:30–32.
A rope of palm fibre is “في جيدها,” staging the section’s dictionary scene of a rope thrown around the neck rather than the rope being removed.
The miser is told not to make his hand “مغلولة إلى عنقك”; withheld wealth appears as the giver’s own hand chained to his neck.
What people hoard from God’s bounty will be collared around them on resurrection, turning possessed wealth into the possessor’s neck-bond.
God places fetters “في أعناق الذين كفروا,” again joining the covering of truth with a bond fixed at the neck.
God announces “أنكالا وجحيما,” fetters together with a blazing fire, the same conjunction of binding and final enclosure.
The criminals are seen “مقرنين في الأصفاد,” coupled together in fetters, an exact collective scene of bodies made fast.
After the fetters of 14:49, fire covers their faces, joining bodily binding to the section’s reversal in which coverers are covered.
They are thrown into a narrow place of the fire “مقرنين,” so confinement and binding reinforce one another spatially.
The sacrificial animals and “القلائد” may not be violated; an animal led by the ه د ي family is marked at the neck by a garland, realizing the section’s link between leading and necks.
The sacrificial animals are “معكوفا” and prevented from reaching their محل, staging a led animal held back before the place where its restriction would end.
The pilgrim must wait “حتى يبلغ الهدي محله”; the هدي animal is led toward the point of release, while obstruction creates ransom, charity, or sacrifice in the same ayah.
The Israelites expel one another and make captives, then ransom those captives although the expulsion itself is forbidden; releasing a captive exposes the contradiction of first fastening the bond.
A wall with a gate divides mercy inside from punishment outside; this threshold shows that a door and enclosure can separate the two final companies.
No ransom is accepted from hypocrites or disbelievers at the wall of 57:13, and the fire is their refuge; the opportunity to buy release has closed.
The criminal wishes to ransom himself from that day’s punishment with his own children, reversing the section’s person who spends to release another.
He would offer everyone on earth if it might save him, carrying the failed ransom of 70:11 to its absolute limit.
“كلا إنها لظى” closes the ransom attempt of 70:11–14: no offered substitute opens a way out of the blaze.
A debtor in hardship must be given respite, and remitting the debt as charity is better; a financial claim that could hold a person is deliberately loosened.
Believers “تواصوا بالصبر” in the exact reciprocal wording used in 90:17, making shared counsel to self-restraint part of the way beyond bondage.
The generous spend in ease and hardship, restrain anger, and pardon people; giving outwardly is paired with binding one’s own impulse rather than another person.
Repelling evil with what is better turns an enemy into a close ally, showing what the section’s inward restraint can release between people.
Only those who are patient receive the transforming response of 41:34, explicitly naming the self-restraint that makes release of hostility possible.
People of means are told not to stop giving to kin, the needy, and emigrants, but to pardon and overlook; wealth and inward restraint jointly release another from deprivation.
Secret alms to the poor are better and God “يكفر عنكم” misdeeds; covering a gift and covering sins are merciful reversals of covering truth and closing wealth away.
God has prescribed “تحلة أيمانكم,” the dissolution of oaths; the section’s حل of a knot becomes release from a binding utterance.
Hearts and hearing are sealed and sight bears a covering, making disbelief a closure of the very faculties by which guidance could enter.
A covering is put over the self-deifier’s sight and the ayah asks who can guide him afterward, explicitly linking covered perception to blocked guidance.
The question whether hearts have “أقفالها” turns refusal to contemplate the Quran into an interior lock.
The one who turns from the reminder has coverings placed over the heart and heaviness in the ears, and cannot reach guidance while that closure persists.
The rejecters themselves claim that their hearts are in coverings, their ears are deaf, and a veil stands between the two sides; their stance voices closure against the call.
Coverings over hearts and heaviness in ears keep listeners from understanding, and even seeing every sign does not open belief.
What people earned has rusted over their hearts, presenting moral accumulation as a covering laid down from within.
The rusted hearts of 83:14 are followed by being veiled from their Lord, making inner covering become final exclusion.
After the rust and veil of 83:14–15, they enter the blaze, completing the movement from self-made covering to punitive enclosure.
The person destined for the closed fire of 104:8 accumulates wealth and keeps counting it, tying the enclosure to wealth kept under the counter’s control.
The wealth-counter is thrown into the Crusher, beginning the punishment whose closed form is named in 104:8.
“The fire of God, kindled” identifies what 104:8 closes over them.
The fire rises over the hearts before it is described as closed over them, making enclosure penetrate the same inward place that truth can be covered.
Hell “لمحيطة بالكافرين,” explicitly enclosing the people who covered truth.
The punishment covers them from above and from beneath their feet, giving the enclosure of 29:54 its vertical completeness.
Hell is a bed beneath the rejecters and coverings above them, a direct fire-enclosure on both sides.
Canopies of fire lie above and below them, rendering the punishment as layered cover.
The unjust are surrounded by a fire whose walls encompass them, making rejection a place from which even a plea for relief brings scalding water.
Whenever the defiantly disobedient try to leave the fire, they are returned to it; desire for release cannot open the enclosure.
Whenever they try to leave the fire’s anguish, they are returned and told to taste the burning, repeating the no-exit boundary.
They wish to leave the fire but cannot leave it, an explicit denial of فك-like escape.
The followers disown their leaders yet “وما هم بخارجين من النار”; severed human ties do not become release from the fire.
The blowers act “في العقد,” a scene of knots being worked for harm rather than the saving untying named by the section.
God expands the breast of one guided to submission but makes the breast of one led astray constricted and cramped, placing openness and closure on the two sides of guidance.
The one whose breast God opens to submission stands in divine light, while the hard-hearted face woe; inner opening reverses the sealed faculties of denial.
Whatever mercy God opens none can withhold, and whatever He withholds none can release afterward; opening and holding are set as opposite sovereign acts.
The heavens and earth were a joined closure and God split them open, a cosmic instance of the section’s basic movement from tight joining to opening.
Holding together to God’s rope saves a formerly hostile people from the brink of fire; here a rope joins for rescue rather than fastening a neck for bondage.
The righteous are given sealed pure drink, so closure preserves a gift rather than imprisoning people in punishment.
The seal of the drink in 83:25 is musk, specifying a fragrant, desirable sealing opposite the section’s punitive lid.
“That they may understand my speech” states what the loosened tongue-knot of 20:27 makes possible: opening restores communication.
Barriers before and behind the neck-fettered people of 36:8 cover them so they cannot see, adding visual enclosure to bodily bondage.
The battle command to strike above the necks is the violent boundary opposite “freeing a neck”; the shared bodily site carries contrary acts.
The Prophet is told to address captives in his hands: God may give them better than what was taken and forgive them, placing material loss and possible inward release together.
A wife may give compensation to obtain release when the couple fear they cannot keep God’s limits, turning payment into an exit from the marriage bond.
Even an earth-full of gold offered as ransom is not accepted from one who dies denying, setting the final limit on wealth’s power to release.
All the earth’s wealth and as much again cannot ransom the disbeliever from the Day’s punishment, while the section spends wealth to free another before that day.
The unjust soul would ransom itself with everything on earth when it sees punishment, but concealed regret cannot buy release.
Those who do not answer their Lord would ransom themselves with the earth twice over, but their destination remains Hell.
Wrongdoers would offer all the earth and its like to ransom themselves when an unforeseen punishment appears; release sought only at enclosure comes too late.
Equivalent retaliation is permitted, yet patience is better; the harmed person’s restraint holds the self back from tightening harm on another.
Patience joined with forgiveness is called a matter of resolve, making self-restraint the condition for releasing another’s offense.
A pilgrim who kills game must send an equivalent domestic animal as “هديا بالغ الكعبة”; the led offering and hunted animal meet in a compensatory neck-and-animal scene.
The Kaaba, sacred month, sacrificial animals, and garlands are made supports for people; the led and neck-marked animal belongs to an ordered sacred boundary.
Joseph is drawn from the well as a boy and immediately hidden as merchandise, showing a child at the threshold of becoming property.
Joseph is sold for a paltry price, completing 12:19’s movement from found child to possessed person and concretizing the source section’s child/slave overlap.
“ولدان مخلدون” circulate in service among the blessed; the Quranic serving youths activate the source section’s ولدان form at the border of child and servant.
Everlasting youths circulate in service, another Quranic use of ولدان that makes the source section’s child/servant lexical overlap visible.
The oath “والليل إذا يغشى” states that night covers, directly staging the dictionary explanation that night can be called kāfir because its darkness conceals.
Night “إذا يغشاها” covers the sun or the scene named by the pronoun, repeating the covering action behind the source section’s secondary night sense.
Night covers Abraham before he examines the star and rejects what sets; darkness becomes the setting from which discernment of truth emerges.
Date palms are “ذات الأكمام,” bearing sheathed fruit; the Quran directly presents the plant-container image used in the section to explain the covering family.
No fruit emerges from its sheath without God’s knowledge, showing the hidden thing opening from its plant-cover.
If believers are mindful, God gives a criterion and “يكفر عنكم سيئاتكم”; covering sins accompanies discernment, opposite the covering that blocks truth.
Believers ask God “كفر عنا سيئاتنا”; the same covering root becomes a plea for sins to be covered rather than truth.
Those who believe the truth have their misdeeds covered by God and their condition repaired, reversing the disbelievers’ covering in 47:1 before the neck-and-release law of 47:4.

The righteous drink a cup mixed with “كافورا”; this is the Quranic kāfūr drink term, not securely the source section’s palm-blossom sheath sense, but the shared dictionary form matters within the same surah’s captive, fetter, and serving-youth scenes.
God fastens each person’s record of deeds to the neck, using the bodily site that represents the whole person for an obligation from which the person cannot detach himself.
The object fastened to the neck in 17:13 becomes an open, outspread book that the person must read; opening exposes accountability rather than releasing it.
“واصبر نفسك” tells the Prophet to hold his own self with the people who call on God, an exact Quranic realization of the source definition “I restrained my self” for صبر.
The assembled wrongdoers and their objects of worship are commanded to be guided to the path of Hell, turning هدى into the leading of captives toward enclosure rather than guidance toward release.

The believers are likened to a seed that strengthens into a crop delighting the sowers, while the same ayah says it enrages “الكفار”; cultivation and the disbelievers’ covering stand deliberately together.
Those dragged by neck-fetters in 40:71 are taken through boiling water and then burned in the fire, completing the bond’s destination.
God guides the human being to the way, after which one is grateful or coveringly ungrateful; 76:4 then turns that response into the boundary between guidance and fetters.
The feeders of the captive in 76:8 say they seek neither repayment nor thanks, identifying the inward restraint that keeps an act of release from becoming a new claim on its recipient.
Because the righteous were patient, God rewards them with garden and silk; in the same surah the rejecters receive fetters, so self-restraint leads away from imposed restraint.
The question “What put you into Saqar?” connects the pledged soul and companions of the right in 74:38–39 to the fire whose causes include refusing to feed the needy in 74:44.
The wealth-counter thinks his wealth will make him immortal; this false confidence explains why accumulated wealth culminates in the closed fire of 104:8.
The criminal would add his wife and brother to the child offered in 70:11, widening the attempted ransom through his closest relations.
He would also offer the clan that sheltered him, completing the circle of human protection he tries unsuccessfully to exchange for release.
The blaze of 70:15 calls the person who turned away, connecting inward refusal to the fire that will not accept his ransom.
The person called by the blaze gathered wealth and shut it away, making his own act of enclosure the conduct answered by enclosing fire.
Failure to honor the orphan begins a rebuke whose sequence ends in God’s incomparable binding, linking withheld care to the bond of 89:26.
The people do not urge one another to feed the needy, the same omission that explains the fettered person’s punishment in 69:34.
They consume inheritance greedily, identifying acquisition without release as part of the conduct judged in the passage.
Their excessive love of wealth completes the withholding scene that culminates in the binding of 89:26.
“No one binds as His binding” gives the orphan-neglecting, wealth-loving passage its final bodily reversal: people who did not loosen need face an unmatched bond.
The warning of a blazing fire begins the outcome paired in this passage with denial and, on the opposite side, purification through giving wealth.
The one who enters the blaze is the one who denied and turned away, joining covering truth to the fire announced in 92:14.
The deeply mindful person is kept away from that fire, opening the passage’s opposite outcome.
The person spared gives his wealth to purify himself, making wealth released outward the counterpart of the denier’s fire.
Those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it in God’s way are promised painful punishment, connecting closed-up wealth to its punitive return.
The hoarded metal is heated in Hell and used to brand its owners, so possessed wealth becomes the instrument that takes possession of their bodies.
The miserly conceal the bounty God gave them and urge others to miserliness; hidden provision and the punishment prepared for coverers meet in one ayah.
Those who consume orphans’ wealth consume fire into their bellies, turning wealth withheld from the vulnerable directly into fire within the withholder.
The fasting concession requires a fidyah consisting of feeding a needy person, so compensatory release from a bodily obligation itself takes the form of releasing another’s hunger.
The marriage “knot” and the choice to forgo a financial half-share stand in one ayah; relinquishing a claim is placed at the boundary of a binding عقدة.
The parable contrasts an owned slave who has no power with a person given good provision who spends it secretly and openly, joining human ownership, wealth, and release of provision.

The ayah places owned servants and children not yet at puberty side by side while distinguishing their privacy rules, clarifying the source section’s ولدان overlap between child and servant without collapsing the two.
The doors are locked around Joseph, yet he restrains himself and refuses the invitation; external enclosure is answered by inward moral restraint.
Joseph and the woman race to the door after the doors were locked in 12:23, making escape toward an opening the bodily continuation of his self-restraint.
The rejecters claim their hearts are wrapped, and the ayah answers that their disbelief has brought God’s curse; covering is both their stated stance and their refusal of belief.
They again claim that their hearts are wrapped, but the ayah says God sealed them because of their disbelief, explicitly joining kufr to inner closure.
God seals the hearts, hearing, and sight of those who prefer the nearer life after belief, closing all three avenues of apprehension.
They believed and then disbelieved, so their hearts were sealed; the sequence makes covering truth the cause of a further inability to understand.
Those who dispute God’s signs without warrant have every arrogant heart sealed; the same surah later shows such disputants dragged by neck-fetters in 40:71.

Even if the condemned endure patiently, the fire remains their lodging, and seeking restoration brings none; patience after enclosure no longer performs the saving self-restraint praised by the section.
The people of the fire are told that whether they endure patiently or not is the same, marking the point at which صبر can no longer alter the bond’s outcome.
The hypothetical sealing of hearing and hearts and removal of sight is followed by the question who besides God could restore them, defining both the closure and the sole power that can open it.
The lasting gardens have their gates opened for the righteous, the welcoming reversal of heavenly gates barred to rejecters and fire closed over them.
Hell’s gates are opened when the disbelievers arrive, showing that an opened door can admit a person into punishment rather than effect release.
They are told to enter Hell’s gates and remain there, making the admission of 39:71 a permanent enclosure.
The mindful are led to the garden and find its gates opened, making opened entry the opposite destiny to the disbelievers’ enduring enclosure.
When people forget the reminder, the gates of everything are opened to them until sudden seizure overtakes their joy; abundance’s opening can itself become the mouth of a trap.
After the condemned person failed to urge feeding the needy in 69:34, he has no food except foul discharge, reversing the feeding he would not support.
The marriage knot may not be resolved before the waiting term reaches its end, using عقدة as a bond whose opening has a divinely set boundary.
On the judgment day described here, no compensating equivalent is accepted and no help is given, setting the final limit on ransom as a means of release.
The repeated warning says no compensating equivalent will be accepted from any soul, reinforcing that the opportunity for costly release belongs before judgment.
The Prophet is warned against taking captives for the nearer world’s goods before the battle is decisively subdued, exposing material gain as a corrupt reason for fastening people.
The command to be patient after 16:126 adds that such self-restraint comes only through God and must not collapse into grief or constriction over opponents.
Although a wrong may receive an equal answer, whoever pardons and repairs has a reward with God; this supplies the releasing act praised as patience and forgiveness in 42:43.
